content.prompt: Identify the corresponding sides and write a similarity statement.

spec.description: Unfilled, similarly oriented right triangles with all printed labels and angle givens. Coordinates establish appearance only and are not additional measurements.
spec.mathematics: A corresponds to R, B to P and C to Q. Right angles occur at A and R; angles C and Q are 40 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied vertex labels, right-angle marks and 40-degree givens are visible.

answer.worked:
The right angles match $A$ with $R$, and the $40^\circ$ angles match $C$ with $Q$, so $B$ matches $P$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ABC&=\angle RPQ\\\angle BCA&=\angle PQR\end{aligned}$$
Corresponding sides are $BC$ and $PQ$, $AC$ and $RQ$, and $AB$ and $RP$.
$$ABC\sim RPQ$$

spec.description: Two unfilled similar pentagons with clipped upper-left corners, larger above smaller. No numerical dimensions are asserted.
spec.mathematics: Corresponding vertices are A/L, B/M, C/N, D/P and E/Q.
spec.answerVisibility: Vertex labels only.

answer.short: $CD\sim NP$, $AE\sim LQ$; $\angle BCD=\angle MNP$, $\angle CDE=\angle NPQ$, $\angle AED=\angle LQP$, $\angle EAB=\angle QLM$; $ABCDE\sim LMNPQ$.
answer.worked:
The corresponding vertices are $A\leftrightarrow L$, $B\leftrightarrow M$, $C\leftrightarrow N$, $D\leftrightarrow P$ and $E\leftrightarrow Q$.
Corresponding sides: $AB\sim LM$, $BC\sim MN$, $CD\sim NP$, $ED\sim QP$, $AE\sim LQ$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ABC&=\angle LMN\\\angle BCD&=\angle MNP\\\angle CDE&=\angle NPQ\\\angle AED&=\angle LQP\\\angle EAB&=\angle QLM\end{aligned}$$
$$ABCDE\sim LMNPQ$$

spec.answerVisibility: All vertex and angle givens remain visible; no response answers are drawn.

answer.short: $DE\sim LK$, $EF\sim KJ$, $FD\sim JL$; $\angle EFD=\angle KJL$, $\angle FDE=\angle JLK$; $DEF\sim LKJ$.
answer.worked:
Match the equal angles: $D\leftrightarrow L$ ($80^\circ$), $E\leftrightarrow K$ ($60^\circ$), $F\leftrightarrow J$ ($40^\circ$).
Corresponding sides: $DE\sim LK$, $EF\sim KJ$, $FD\sim JL$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle DEF&=\angle LKJ\\\angle EFD&=\angle KJL\\\angle FDE&=\angle JLK\end{aligned}$$
$$DEF\sim LKJ$$

answer.short: $MP\sim VU$, $PN\sim UT$, $NM\sim TV$; $\angle MPN=\angle VUT$, $\angle PNM=\angle UTV$, $\angle NMP=\angle TVU$; $MPN\sim VUT$.
answer.worked:
The double arcs match $P$ with $U$, and the single arcs match $N$ with $T$, so $M$ matches $V$.
Corresponding sides: $MP\sim VU$, $PN\sim UT$, $NM\sim TV$.
$$\begin{aligned}\angle MPN&=\angle VUT\\\angle PNM&=\angle UTV\\\angle NMP&=\angle TVU\end{aligned}$$
$$MPN\sim VUT$$

answer.short: $AB\sim GH$, $BC\sim HI$, $CA\sim IG$; $\angle CAB=\angle IGH$, $\angle ABC=\angle GHI$, $\angle BCA=\angle HIG$; $ABC\sim GHI$.
answer.worked:
The right-angle markers match $A$ with $G$, and the dots match $B$ with $H$. Therefore $C$ matches $I$.
$$\begin{aligned}AB&\sim GH\\BC&\sim HI\\CA&\sim IG\\\angle CAB&=\angle IGH\\\angle ABC&=\angle GHI\\\angle BCA&=\angle HIG\end{aligned}$$
Thus $ABC\sim GHI$.

answer.short: $AB\sim MN$, $BC\sim NO$, $CA\sim OM$; $\angle ACB=\angle MON$, $\angle CAB=\angle OMN$, $\angle CBA=\angle ONM$; $ABC\sim MNO$.
answer.worked:
The dots match $A$ with $M$, and the crosses match $C$ with $O$. Therefore $B$ matches $N$.
$$\begin{aligned}AB&\sim MN\\BC&\sim NO\\CA&\sim OM\\\angle ACB&=\angle MON\\\angle CAB&=\angle OMN\\\angle CBA&=\angle ONM\end{aligned}$$
Thus $ABC\sim MNO$.

answer.short: $AD\sim AB$, $DE\sim BC$, $EA\sim CA$; $\angle ADE=\angle ABC$, $\angle DEA=\angle BCA$, $\angle EAD=\angle CAB$; $ADE\sim ABC$.
answer.worked:
Consider triangles $ADE$ and $ABC$. The dots match $D$ with $B$. The angles at $A$ are vertically opposite; $ED\parallel BC$ matches $E$ with $C$.
$$\begin{aligned}AD&\sim AB\\DE&\sim BC\\EA&\sim CA\\\angle ADE&=\angle ABC\\\angle DEA&=\angle BCA\\\angle EAD&=\angle CAB\end{aligned}$$
Thus $ADE\sim ABC$.

inlines.text: (Hint: Redraw the diagram as two triangles)

answer.short: $AB\sim AC$, $AE\sim AD$, $EB\sim DC$; $\angle EAB=\angle DAC$, $\angle EBA=\angle DCA$, $\angle AEB=\angle ADC$; $ABE\sim ACD$.
answer.worked:
Consider triangles $ABE$ and $ACD$. They share the angle at $A$. Since $BE\parallel CD$, corresponding angles match $B$ with $C$ and $E$ with $D$.
$$\begin{aligned}AB&\sim AC\\AE&\sim AD\\EB&\sim DC\\\angle EAB&=\angle DAC\\\angle EBA&=\angle DCA\\\angle AEB&=\angle ADC\end{aligned}$$
Thus $ABE\sim ACD$.

Matching angles give $A\leftrightarrow E$, $B\leftrightarrow F$ and $C\leftrightarrow D$, so $ABC\sim EFD$.

The right angles match $R$ to $V$, and the $37^\circ$ angles match $Q$ to $U$. Hence $RPQ\sim VWU$.

children.prompt: Using angle relationships, show that $ABC$ and $ADE$ are similar.

answer.short: $\angle ABC=\angle ADE$ and $\angle ACB=\angle AED$ (corresponding angles, $BC\parallel DE$). $\angle BAC=\angle DAE$ (common angle). Hence $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle ADE$.
answer.worked:
$\angle ABC=\angle ADE$ (corresponding angles on parallel lines).

$\angle ACB=\angle AED$ (corresponding angles on parallel lines).

$\angle BAC=\angle DAE$ (common angle).

Therefore $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle ADE$, since all corresponding angles are equal.

spec.description: Triangle with an internal horizontal segment parallel to the base; retain the redundant lower-right 5 cm given.

answer.worked:
The triangles are similar because the marked sides are parallel. The whole left side is $9+3=12\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{6}&=\frac{12}{9}\\x&=6\times\frac{12}{9}\\x&=8\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The triangles are similar because the marked sides are parallel. The whole base is $9+6=15\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{9}&=\frac{6}{15}\\x&=9\times\frac{6}{15}\\x&=3.6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

The triangles are similar because the marked sides are parallel.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x+6}{6}&=\frac{15}{6}\\x+6&=6\times\frac{15}{6}\\x+6&=15\\x&=9\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
A map is drawn to scale, on 1-cm paper, showing the position of a supermarket and a cinema.

It takes 10 minutes to walk in a straight line from the cinema to the supermarket at a constant speed of 3 km/h. Show that the scale of the map is $1\text{ cm}=100\text{ m}$.

spec.description: Seven-column, two-row square grid with Cinema on the first internal vertical line and Supermarket on the sixth, both on the middle horizontal line. A blank-grid template cannot express the required labelled point markers.
spec.mathematics: Each grid interval represents 1 cm on the map. The points are five horizontal intervals apart, so their map distance is 5 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: The grid, both points and both labels are permanent student-visible givens; no solution marks are included.

answer.short: The actual distance is $500\text{ m}$ and the map distance is $5\text{ cm}$, so $1\text{ cm}$ represents $100\text{ m}$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Time}&=\frac{10}{60}\text{ h}=\frac16\text{ h}\\\text{Actual distance}&=3\times\frac16\text{ km}\\&=0.5\text{ km}\\&=500\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
The points are five grid intervals apart, so their map distance is $5\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Distance represented by }1\text{ cm}&=\frac{500}{5}\text{ m}\\&=100\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

[Pedagogy review · High priority · unsupported-transition · pf-d85496d561]
Finding: The rectangle demonstration does not supply the grid-construction method needed for the first sloping-sided figures.
Breakdown: Students can multiply the parallelogram's horizontal side and height correctly while retaining its original one-square horizontal displacement. The resulting figure has different angles. Multiplying side lengths and stating that angles must remain equal do not show how to position the new vertices.
Checked: The preceding teaching explains correspondence, equal angles and multiplying lengths. Neither p12-scale-factor-figures nor the rectangle example demonstrates scaling horizontal and vertical displacements along a sloping edge.
Assumes: Elementary grid counting is prior knowledge; constructing enlargements by scaling vertex displacements is not established. Calculator use does not affect this issue.
Also affects: p13-q1-a, p13-q1-b
Proposed repair (add-teaching): Before p13-q1-a, show a miniature grid example: “This edge moves 1 square right and 3 squares up. At scale factor 2, multiply both moves by 2: move 2 squares right and 6 squares up.” Draw the original and enlarged edge, then state that the same method positions the other vertices.
Done when: A sloping-edge construction explicitly scales both grid displacements before students construct the parallelogram.

Add only this instruction: “Predict whether each image will be smaller, congruent or larger before drawing.” (i) Scale factor 0.5. Answer: 2 by 1 squares, smaller. (j) Scale factor 1. Answer: 4 by 2 squares, congruent. (k) Scale factor 1.5. Answer: 6 by 3 squares, larger. (l) Scale factor 2. Answer: 8 by 4 squares, larger. Follow with an unpatterned part (m), scale factor 0.75. Finding: The parallel-line triangle questions precede the teaching that equal corresponding angles are sufficient for triangle similarity.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · unsupported-transition · pf-857ef845f3]
Finding: The shared-side trapezia require a proportion that cannot follow the instruction to always place the unknown in the numerator.
Breakdown: The stated correspondence gives x/7 = 63/x, or its reciprocal. Either choice puts x in a denominator. The preceding models do not explain this exception or the resulting squared unknown, leaving students without a route consistent with the advertised method.
Checked: BC ↔ EF and EF ↔ AD give x/7 = 63/x. For a positive length, multiplying by 7x gives x² = 441 and x = 21 cm. Earlier teaching and practice do not model a shared length occupying both correspondence roles.
Assumes: Basic equation solving and square roots may be prior knowledge from the separate algebra booklets. The finding concerns the conflicting instruction and this new similarity setup, not unsupported arithmetic.
Also affects: p34-q5-root
Proposed repair (add-teaching): Change the p30 instruction to “Where possible, put the unknown in the numerator to make the equation easier to solve.” Beside Q5, add: “BC ↔ EF and EF ↔ AD, so x/7 = 63/x. The shared length occurs in both ratios, so it cannot appear only in numerators. Multiplying both sides by 7x gives x² = 7 × 63 = 441. A length is positive, so x = 21 cm.”
Done when: The instruction allows the necessary exception, and the shared-side proportion is explicitly connected to its positive solution.

entries.description: Finding Lengths in Scale Drawings

Scale Drawings
A scale drawing is a smaller or larger drawing of a real-life object.
Examples include maps, house plans, and scientific diagrams.
We call the real-life object the original, and the drawing the image.
Scales for scale drawings are written in simplified ratio notation:

image : original
1 : n
